claims.text: Introducing a nanometer-scale RHEA interfacial coating between tungsten and copper increases the effective thermal conductivity of a W–Cu composite.
The RHEA interfacial coating allows the W–Cu composite to retain mechanical durability.
The RHEA interfacial coating allows the W–Cu composite to retain irradiation resistance.
The proposed intervention is to deposit a thin, well-adhered RHEA interlayer or disperse RHEA nanoparticles at the W–Cu interface during fabrication.
Temperatures of 500–700 °C and fusion-relevant irradiation represent the application conditions under which the improvement is expected.
A nanocrystalline RHEA layer refines the W–Cu interfacial microstructure.
A nanocrystalline RHEA layer reduces thermal boundary resistance at the W–Cu interface.
A nanocrystalline RHEA layer improves bonding between tungsten and copper.
Nanocrystalline RHEAs can exhibit high thermal stability.
Nanocrystalline RHEAs can exhibit resistance to heavy-ion irradiation, dual-beam irradiation, and helium implantation.
The RHEA interlayer minimizes irradiation-induced defect accumulation at the W–Cu interface.
The RHEA interlayer provides enhanced electron-transport pathways across the W–Cu interface.
The RHEA interlayer provides enhanced phonon-transport pathways across the W–Cu interface.
Reduced interfacial resistance produces a measurable increase in effective thermal conductivity without compromising mechanical strength.
Relative to an otherwise identical uncoated W–Cu composite, the coated composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity.
Relative to the control, the coated composite will show no reduction in mechanical durability or irradiation resistance.
The magnitude of the conductivity increase and the long-term stability of the interlayer under cyclic thermal and irradiation exposure remain uncertain.
